title: Seasonal influenza vaccination coverage and population health burden in Europe during the 2019/2020 and 2021/2022 influenza seasons: an ecological panel analysis using principal-component-adjusted multivariable regression.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Few studies have examined whether country-level seasonal influenza vaccination coverage is associated with population health burden.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted an ecological panel analysis using SHARE Waves 8 (2019-2020) and 9 (2021-2022) across participating EU/EEA countries, Switzerland, and Israel.
analysis.methods: We derived survey-weighted vaccination coverage and structural indicators among adults aged ≥55 years. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the pooled country-season dataset to summarize correlated structural covariates. Associations were estimated using linear mixed-effects models with country-specific random intercepts.
analysis.main_results: Mean vaccination coverage increased from 34.5% to 47.6% but remained below the EU target of 75% in many countries. A 1-percentage-point higher vaccination coverage was associated with 14.9 fewer all-cause deaths per 100,000 adults aged ≥55 years (95% CI: -22.8 to -7.1), 328.1 fewer all-cause DALYs per 100,000 (95% CI: -480.4 to -175.8), and 6.3 fewer LRTI DALYs per 100,000 (95% CI: -10.6 to -2.0).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: In this two-period ecological analysis, higher country-level influenza vaccination coverage was inversely associated with mortality and DALY burden among adults aged ≥55 years. These findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating population-level associations rather than causal effects.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that increasing influenza vaccination coverage could reduce mortality and DALY burden among older adults, which could inform public health strategies and policy.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study design limitations include the ecological nature of the analysis, which cannot establish causality. The sample size and generalizability may also be limited.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the associations of influenza vaccination coverage with population health burden in Europe during the 2019/2020 and 2021/2022 influenza seasons. Higher vaccination coverage was inversely associated with mortality and DALY burden among adults aged ≥55 years, suggesting potential public health benefits.

title: Limited added benefit of seasonal influenza vaccination before A(H5) vaccination in mice and ferrets challenged with A(H5N1).

analysis.research_question_and_background: Limited A(H5)-specific vaccine supply is expected early in a potential A(H5N1) pandemic, raising the question of whether licensed seasonal influenza vaccines could enhance protection when administered before A(H5) vaccination.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We evaluated this strategy in mouse and ferret models using clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) viruses.
analysis.methods: Seasonal influenza vaccination induced antibodies to seasonal haemagglutinins but did not induce detectable antibodies against A(H5) and did not consistently enhance A(H5)-directed antibody responses after A(H5) vaccination.
analysis.main_results: In lethal challenge studies, seasonal vaccine priming before A(H5) vaccination was associated with improved outcomes compared with A(H5) vaccination alone in one of three mouse experiments, but this effect was not observed in the other two mouse experiments or in ferrets.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings suggest that seasonal influenza vaccine priming provides limited added benefit to A(H5) vaccine-mediated protection against A(H5N1) under the conditions tested.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the potential utility of seasonal influenza vaccines in augmenting A(H5N1) vaccine efficacy during early pandemic phases, but caution against overreliance on this strategy.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its use of animal models and the inconsistent results across experiments, which may affect generalisability to human populations.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates whether seasonal influenza vaccines could enhance protection against A(H5N1) when administered before A(H5) vaccination. Using mouse and ferret models, the research found that seasonal vaccine priming improved outcomes in one of three mouse experiments but not in others or in ferrets. The results suggest limited added benefit of seasonal vaccines in this context. The study's significance lies in its implications for pandemic preparedness, but its reliance on animal models and inconsistent findings highlight limitations in generalisability to humans.

title: Multifocal mucocutaneous herpes simplex virus type 1 infection temporally associated with seasonal influenza vaccination in a young adult without a known immunocompromising condition: A case report.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate a case of multifocal mucocutaneous Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection temporally associated with seasonal influenza vaccination in a young adult without a known immunocompromising condition, addressing the rare immunological adverse events reported with seasonal influenza vaccination.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A case report was conducted in a 28-year-old man without a known immunocompromising condition, following seasonal influenza vaccination.
analysis.methods: HSV-1 DNA was detected in specimens from clinically apparent lesions using a multiplex polymerase chain reaction assay, while other sexually transmitted pathogens were not detected.
analysis.main_results: Seven days after vaccination, the patient developed oral ulcerative lesions and multiple vesicular eruptions involving the anterior chest wall, pubic region, and penile shaft. HSV-1 DNA was detected in the lesions, but HSV-2 and other sexually transmitted pathogens were not detected.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Although causality cannot be established, the close temporal relationship between influenza vaccination and the onset of HSV-1 infection is noteworthy, while alternative explanations cannot be excluded.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This case highlights the importance of considering HSV infection in the differential diagnosis of multifocal mucocutaneous lesions occurring after influenza vaccination, without implying a causal relationship.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The case report design limits the strength of evidence, and alternative explanations for the HSV-1 infection cannot be excluded.

analysis.summary_en: A case report describes a 28-year-old man developing multifocal mucocutaneous HSV-1 infection seven days after seasonal influenza vaccination, highlighting the need to consider HSV infection in differential diagnosis without implying causality.

title: Seasonal influenza vaccine strain selection by quantifying viral fitness

analysis.research_question_and_background: The long-standing challenge of seasonal influenza vaccines providing poor protection is attributed to the rapid and continuous evolution of the virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population.
analysis.methods: Furthermore, FutureFlu significantly outperforms the currently used methods in vaccine strain selection whether or not there is available antigenic data from hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay, which provides a valuable supplement for WHO vaccine recommendation.
analysis.main_results: The fitness scores of influenza variants present strong positive correlation with their actual observed frequencies in the next seasons.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: To support global public health implementation, an open online platform (futureflu.com.cn) has been established to offer real-time viral fitness predictions and vaccine recommendations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Validation across 24 seasons of three influenza subtypes shows FutureFlu recommends antigenically matched vaccine strains more frequently than annual recommendations, particularly for challenging subtypes: 83.3% versus 45.8% seasons for A/H3N2, and 75.0% versus 33.3% seasons for B/Victoria.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This deterministic extraction is based on retrieved fulltext evidence. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

analysis.summary_en: The long-standing challenge of seasonal influenza vaccines providing poor protection is attributed to the rapid and continuous evolution of the virus. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population. Furthermore, FutureFlu significantly outperforms the currently used methods in vaccine strain selection whether or not there is available antigenic data from hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay, which provides a valuable supplement for WHO vaccine recommendation. The fitness scores of influenza variants present strong positive correlation with their actual observed frequencies in the next seasons. To support global public health implementation, an open online platform (futureflu.com.cn) has been established to offer real-time viral fitness predictions and vaccine recommendations. Validation across 24 seasons of three influenza subtypes shows FutureFlu recommends antigenically matched vaccine strains more frequently than annual recommendations, particularly for challenging subtypes: 83.3% versus 45.8% seasons for A/H3N2, and 75.0% versus 33.3% seasons for B/Victoria. This deterministic extraction is based on retrieved fulltext evidence. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

title: VirPLM: Antigenic prediction of influenza A/H3N2 viruses with a fine-tuned protein language model.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenge of antigenic prediction for influenza A/H3N2 viruses, which undergo rapid antigenic evolution due to immune pressure-induced amino acid substitutions in the hemagglutinin subunit 1 (HA1).
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study presents a two-stage framework, VirPLM, which adapts the ESM-2 protein language model to H3N2 HA1 sequences for antigenic prediction, and evaluates its performance across cross-validation and retrospective time-split analyses.
analysis.methods: The methods involve fine-tuning the ESM-2 protein language model on H3N2 HA1 sequences to predict antigenic properties, and assessing its performance using cross-validation and retrospective time-split evaluations.
analysis.main_results: The results show that VirPLM significantly outperforms representative methods and maintains robust performance under both cross-validation and retrospective time-split evaluations.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these findings as demonstrating the effectiveness of VirPLM in antigenic prediction for H3N2 viruses, identifying highly critical sites related to antigenic evolution that are enriched in known regions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that VirPLM can provide complementary sequence-based evidence for candidate strain prioritization, potentially improving the accuracy and efficiency of vaccine strain selection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is strong, but the framework's performance was evaluated only on H3N2 sequences, limiting generalizability to other influenza subtypes or lineages.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces VirPLM, a two-stage framework that fine-tunes the ESM-2 protein language model on H3N2 HA1 sequences to predict antigenic properties. The research addresses the challenge of antigenic evolution in influenza A/H3N2 viruses, driven by immune pressure-induced amino acid substitutions in HA1. The methods involve adapting the model for antigenic prediction and evaluating its performance through cross-validation and retrospective time-split analyses. The main results indicate that VirPLM significantly outperforms existing methods and identifies critical sites related to antigenic evolution. The authors interpret these results as demonstrating the potential of VirPLM to improve vaccine strain prioritization by providing complementary sequence-based evidence. The scientific significance lies in its ability to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of antigenic prediction for seasonal influenza viruses, which could inform better surveillance and vaccine development. However, the study's limitations include the exclusive focus on H3N2 sequences, which may restrict generalizability to other influenza subtypes.

title: Bovine mammary tissues are susceptible to infection by viruses bearing panzootic H5N1 influenza A virus glycoproteins

analysis.research_question_and_background: The emergence of the panzootic clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza in 2020 expanded the host range of influenza A viruses, raising concerns about cross‐species transmission and zoonotic spillover, and the study aimed to determine whether mammary tissue from cattle could be infected by viruses bearing H5N1 glycoproteins.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The investigators used mammary gland explants from Aberdeen Angus, Holstein Friesian and Limousin cattle, inoculating the tissues with attenuated reassortant viruses expressing the HA and NA of three 2.3.4.4b viruses that predated the emergence of H5N1 in US cattle.
analysis.methods: Mammary explants were inoculated with reassortant viruses, and infection was assessed by immunohistochemistry for viral NP antigen and lectin staining for α2,3‐ and α2,6‐linked sialic acids.
analysis.main_results: Immunohistochemistry detected viral NP antigen in both the teat and gland cistern of all three breeds following inoculation with AIV09 and AIV48, and lectin staining revealed expression of both α2,3‐ and α2,6‐linked sialic acids in all donor tissues.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings demonstrate that bovine mammary tissue is susceptible to infection by viruses bearing H5N1 glycoproteins and may provide an environment for co‐infection of diverse influenza A viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results underscore the need to include both beef and dairy cattle in H5N1 surveillance and risk‐assessment frameworks, as bovine mammary glands could serve as a reservoir for influenza A virus evolution.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations.

analysis.summary_en: The study investigated whether bovine mammary tissue could be infected by influenza A viruses bearing H5N1 glycoproteins, a concern heightened by the 2020 emergence of the panzootic clade 2.3.4.4b. Using explants from three cattle breeds, researchers inoculated tissues with reassortant viruses expressing HA and NA from pre‐US‐cattle H5N1 strains. Infection was confirmed by immunohistochemistry detecting viral NP antigen in both teat and gland cistern tissues, and lectin staining showed that all breeds expressed both avian‐ and mammalian‐linked sialic acids, the receptors for influenza A virus. These results demonstrate that bovine mammary tissue is susceptible to H5N1‐bearing viruses and could support co‐infection of diverse influenza A strains. Consequently, the findings highlight the importance of incorporating beef and dairy cattle into ongoing H5N1 surveillance and risk‐assessment efforts.

title: Ubiquitination in influenza a virus-host interactions

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on the interaction mechanisms between key amino acid residues of Influenza A virus (IAV)-encoded proteins undergoing ubiquitination and host proteins, as well as the effects of experimental mutations. The central question is to deeply elucidate the interaction between influenza virus and the host.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic analysis of the mechanisms of interaction between IAV-encoded proteins and host proteins related to ubiquitination. It includes experimental mutations and their effects, aiming to understand the molecular interactions involved in IAV-host interactions.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Ubiquitination is a crucial host antiviral defense mechanism that plays a significant role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and internal balance. The review highlights the importance of ubiquitination in the interaction between IAV and host proteins, particularly through the modification of key amino acid residues in IAV-encoded proteins.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that mutation of gene sites in IAV-encoded proteins is a crucial mechanism for viral evolution and adaptation to the host environment. However, the evidence is limited in terms of specific mechanisms and their implications, indicating a need for further research.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that understanding the role of ubiquitination in IAV-host interactions could lead to new strategies for antiviral interventions. It emphasizes the need for more detailed studies on the molecular mechanisms of ubiquitination and its impact on viral evolution and host defense.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the role of ubiquitination in the interaction between Influenza A virus (IAV) and host proteins, focusing on key amino acid residues in IAV-encoded proteins and their effects on viral evolution and adaptation. The study highlights the importance of ubiquitination as a host defense mechanism and identifies gaps in understanding specific molecular interactions. The findings suggest potential avenues for research and antiviral strategies targeting these interactions.

title: ATG13 promotes K63-linked polyubiquitination of MAVS via ASB1 to restrict influenza A virus replication.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the function and mechanism of action of ATG13 during influenza virus infection, as its role in regulating the autophagy initiation complex is well established, but its specific involvement in influenza virus replication remains unclear.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study focused on influenza A virus (IAV) and influenza B virus, examining their interactions with ATG13 in the context of antiviral innate immunity. The research was conducted using molecular and cellular approaches to elucidate the mechanism of ATG13's immunomodulatory function.
analysis.methods: The study employed coimmunoprecipitation assays to investigate the interaction between ATG13 and MAVS, and dual-luciferase reporter assays combined with pharmacological inhibition of autophagy to confirm the independence of ATG13's function from the canonical autophagy pathway.
analysis.main_results: Coimmunoprecipitation assays revealed that ATG13 interacts with MAVS and recruits the E3 ubiquitin ligase ASB1 to catalyze K63-linked polyubiquitination at the K348 residue, thereby amplifying the downstream antiviral signalling cascade.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identifies ATG13 as a novel host restriction factor against IAV and reveals a nonautophagic role for ATG13 in antiviral innate immunity, providing new insights into its function during influenza virus infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings contribute to understanding the host factors that restrict influenza A virus replication and may inform the development of novel therapeutic strategies targeting the type I interferon pathway.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro and molecular analyses, and further in vivo studies are needed to confirm the broader implications of ATG13's role in antiviral immunity. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the lack of clinical or epidemiological data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of ATG13 in influenza virus infection, revealing its function as a host restriction factor against influenza A virus (IAV). The research demonstrates that ATG13 interacts with MAVS and recruits ASB1 to catalyze K63-linked polyubiquitination, thereby enhancing antiviral signaling. The findings highlight a nonautophagic mechanism of ATG13 in innate immunity, offering new insights into host-virus interactions. However, the study is limited to in vitro experiments, and further research is needed to validate these results in vivo. The evidence is moderate, as it does not include clinical or epidemiological data.

title: Immunogenetic determinants of influenza B virus susceptibility and vaccine response: current evidence, gaps, and future directions

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza B virus (IBV) remains an important but comparatively underexamined contributor to seasonal influenza burden, particularly in children, adolescents, and older adults. Although IBV lacks the broad animal reservoir and pandemic potential of influenza A virus, its epidemiology, evolutionary dynamics, and contribution to variable vaccine effectiveness remain clinically and biologically important.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This review evaluates current evidence for immunogenetic determinants of IBV susceptibility and vaccine response, distinguishing direct IBV findings from conclusions extrapolated from influenza A virus or general antiviral immunology.
analysis.methods: Available evidence identifies antigenic match, antigenic drift, age, exposure history, and baseline immunity as the best-supported non-genetic determinants of vaccine performance, whereas IBV-specific host-genetic predictors of susceptibility and vaccine response remain incompletely defined.
analysis.main_results: Recent surveillance has further changed the field: no confirmed naturally circulating B/Yamagata-lineage viruses have been detected since March 2020, and current influenza B activity is overwhelmingly attributable to B/Victoria-lineage viruses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors highlight the major evidence gaps that limit predictive models of IBV immune control and vaccine performance, and outline priorities for future research, including integrated studies linking host genotype, immune phenotyping, and lineage-resolved virologic outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of more accurate predictive models for IBV immune control and vaccine performance, emphasizing the need for integrated studies that connect host genetics with virologic outcomes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The strength of evidence varies across these domains, and much of the proposed framework still relies on inference from broader influenza literature rather than direct IBV-specific human data.

analysis.summary_en: This review addresses the underexamined role of influenza B virus (IBV) in seasonal influenza burden, particularly in children, adolescents, and older adults. It evaluates current evidence on immunogenetic determinants of IBV susceptibility and vaccine response, distinguishing findings specific to IBV from those extrapolated from influenza A virus or general antiviral immunology. The study highlights that while antigenic match, antigenic drift, age, exposure history, and baseline immunity are well-supported non-genetic factors influencing vaccine performance, IBV-specific host-genetic predictors remain poorly defined. Recent surveillance indicates that B/Victoria-lineage viruses dominate current influenza B activity, with no confirmed B/Yamagata-lineage viruses since March 2020. The authors emphasize the need for integrated studies linking host genotype, immune phenotyping, and lineage-resolved virologic outcomes to improve predictive models for IBV immune control and vaccine effectiveness. However, the evidence is limited by reliance on broader influenza literature rather than direct IBV-specific human data, which affects the strength of conclusions.

title: Streamlined CRISPR-based assays for detection and subtyping of H5 and H7 avian influenza

analysis.research_question_and_background: Avian influenza viruses (AIVs) are zoonotic pathogens that pose an increasing global threat due to their potential for significant economic losses in agriculture, and the risk of a pandemic should human-to-human transmission occur. In light of this, we need rapid, sensitive, and specific tests to detect and differentiate circulating AIVs.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study developed three CRISPR-based Streamlined Highlighting of Infections to Navigate Epidemics (SHINE) assays to address the limitations of current AIV diagnostic methods. These assays were designed, optimized, and validated using seasonal-influenza-positive clinical samples.
analysis.methods: We designed, optimized, and validated a SHINE assay for H5 AIV, achieving 100% specificity when tested on seasonal-influenza-positive clinical samples, and a limit of detection of 121.7 copies/μL. We also developed SHINE assays targeting the 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) and Eurasian H7 lineages.
analysis.main_results: The SHINE assay for H5 AIV achieved 100% specificity when tested on seasonal-influenza-positive clinical samples, and a limit of detection of 121.7 copies/μL. The SHINE assays for 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) and Eurasian H7 lineages were also developed.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Together, these SHINE assays offer a promising platform for AIV diagnosis and surveillance, particularly outside laboratory settings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These assays provide a rapid, sensitive, and specific diagnostic tool for AIVs, which can enhance surveillance and early detection in low-resource settings and improve public health preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study does not report limitations, but the evidence is based on a single assay validation and does not include broader testing or comparison with other diagnostic methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces three CRISPR-based SHINE assays for the detection and subtyping of avian influenza viruses (AIVs), specifically targeting H5 and H7 lineages. The research was motivated by the need for rapid, sensitive, and specific diagnostic tools for AIVs, which are zoonotic pathogens with significant economic and pandemic risks. The SHINE assays were designed, optimized, and validated using seasonal-influenza-positive clinical samples, achieving 100% specificity and a limit of detection of 121.7 copies/μL for the H5 assay. The assays offer a promising platform for AIV diagnosis and surveillance, particularly in field and low-resource settings. The study does not report limitations, but the evidence is based on a single assay validation and does not include broader testing or comparison with other diagnostic methods. The findings suggest that these assays could improve surveillance and early detection of AIVs, contributing to public health preparedness.

title: TRIM62 facilitates influenza A virus entry by regulating WASH-dependent endosomal trafficking

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how the balance between permissive and inhibitory functions during endocytic uptake is enforced, particularly in the context of influenza A virus entry.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used influenza A virus (IAV) as a model cargo to investigate the role of the WASH complex in viral endocytosis, focusing on the interactions between WASH subunits and the retromer complex.
analysis.methods: The researchers examined the functional roles of WASH subunits, particularly FAM21 and WASH1, in relation to the retromer subunit VPS35, and explored how TRIM62 modulates these interactions to influence IAV entry.
analysis.main_results: The findings indicate that FAM21-mediated association of WASH with VPS35 restricts WASH's pro-endocytic activity, thereby limiting viral uptake, while TRIM62 counteracts this by maintaining WASH in a retromer-free state that promotes viral internalization.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that TRIM62 plays a critical role in modulating the inhibitory effects of FAM21-VPS35 on WASH, thereby facilitating productive IAV entry, which represents a novel mechanism in viral endocytosis.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform the development of targeted therapies or interventions that disrupt WASH-mediated viral entry, potentially improving strategies for combating seasonal influenza.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro and cell-based experiments, and the evidence is based on functional assays and molecular interactions, which may not fully capture in vivo complexities, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of the WASH complex in influenza A virus (IAV) entry, revealing that FAM21-mediated interactions with VPS35 inhibit WASH's pro-endocytic activity, while TRIM62 counteracts this to facilitate viral internalization. The research highlights a novel mechanism involving TRIM62 in modulating WASH function during IAV uptake, with implications for understanding viral entry dynamics. However, the study is limited to in vitro experiments, which may not fully reflect in vivo conditions, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment. The findings contribute to the broader understanding of lipid raft-mediated endocytosis and may inform future therapeutic strategies targeting viral entry pathways.

title: ATTITUDES AND PRACTICES TOWARDS COVID-19 AND SEASONAL FLU VACCINES AND VACCINATION IN THE GENERAL POPULATION AND AMONG MEDICAL PROFESSIONALS

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate attitudes towards COVID-19 and seasonal influenza vaccination among the general population and individuals with a medical background.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Participants generally expressed favourable attitudes towards regular COVID-19 vaccination. The profile of the typical participant was an employed woman with tertiary education, living with another person in an urban area and reporting generally good health.
analysis.methods: A questionnaire was developed to collect sociodemographic data, personal health information, vaccination status, and information on participants’ attitudes towards and knowledge of vaccines.
analysis.main_results: The results showed no apparent differences between participants with and without a medical background regarding vaccine choice, the decision to receive a third dose, or seasonal influenza vaccination.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that attitudes towards vaccination are similar across medical professionals and the general population, highlighting a novel observation about public perception of vaccines.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform public health strategies by suggesting that targeted communication efforts may not need to differentiate between medical professionals and the general population in promoting vaccination.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and its abstract-only nature, which may affect the strength of the evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated attitudes towards COVID-19 and seasonal influenza vaccination among the general population and medical professionals. It found that there were no apparent differences in vaccine choice, third-dose decisions, or seasonal influenza vaccination between the two groups. The research highlights the importance of understanding public perception of vaccines, which can inform public health strategies. However, the study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and its abstract-only nature, which may affect the reliability of the findings. The results suggest that attitudes towards vaccination are consistent across different professional backgrounds, indicating a potential for uniform messaging in health promotion.

title: Modeling the interferon response to avian influenza

analysis.research_question_and_background: Highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses, such as H5N1, cause severe disease in humans and pose a persistent pandemic threat, yet the mechanism by which the type I interferon response shapes their within-host dynamics remains unclear.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population.
analysis.methods: Although the refractory-state model attains the lowest residual error in most conditions, the small-sample-corrected Akaike information criterion does not justify its additional parameter, and the two alternative mechanisms, reduction of infection rate or reduction of production rate, describe the data comparably well.
analysis.main_results: The bootstrapped parameter distributions are largely similar across strains when compared with a Mann-Whitney U-test, differing mainly in the rate of interferon clearance, with only modest differences between the nasal and tracheal epithelium.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These results quantify the interferon response to avian influenza in human respiratory tissue and underscore the need for more frequently sampled data to resolve the dominant mechanism of interferon action in vivo.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: While a structural identifiability analysis suggests all parameters are globally identifiable when both viral titer and interferon are observed, with only ten observations per condition the data cannot single out one mechanism of interferon action.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This deterministic extraction is based on abstract only. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

analysis.summary_en: Highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses, such as H5N1, cause severe disease in humans and pose a persistent pandemic threat, yet the mechanism by which the type I interferon response shapes their within-host dynamics remains unclear. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population. Although the refractory-state model attains the lowest residual error in most conditions, the small-sample-corrected Akaike information criterion does not justify its additional parameter, and the two alternative mechanisms, reduction of infection rate or reduction of production rate, describe the data comparably well. The bootstrapped parameter distributions are largely similar across strains when compared with a Mann-Whitney U-test, differing mainly in the rate of interferon clearance, with only modest differences between the nasal and tracheal epithelium. These results quantify the interferon response to avian influenza in human respiratory tissue and underscore the need for more frequently sampled data to resolve the dominant mechanism of interferon action in vivo. While a structural identifiability analysis suggests all parameters are globally identifiable when both viral titer and interferon are observed, with only ten observations per condition the data cannot single out one mechanism of interferon action. This deterministic extraction is based on abstract only. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

title: Innovation, development, and licensure of improved influenza vaccines: the way forward.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on seasonal influenza viruses, specifically human influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria, as well as the historical B/Yamagata lineage. The central question is about the development and licensure of improved influenza vaccines to address public health needs for pandemic and seasonal influenza.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a general overview of the progress made in achieving the objectives outlined in the Influenza Vaccines R&D Roadmap (IVR) Initiative. It does not report specific databases, search dates, eligibility criteria, or a meta-analysis process.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that without significant improvements in vaccine performance (efficacy, durability, ability to block virus transmission) and production (manufacturing speed, scale-up capacity, adaptability), we risk having to fight the next influenza pandemic with last century's technology.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights the remaining barriers to advanced vaccine development for global use against seasonal and pandemic influenza, but it does not specify conflicting findings or evidence gaps in detail.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The report reviews the remaining barriers to advanced development of vaccines for global use against seasonal and pandemic influenza and summarizes key priorities and activities for moving the influenza vaccine R&D enterprise forward.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on the development and licensure of improved influenza vaccines to address the public health need for pandemic and seasonal influenza. It highlights the progress made in achieving the objectives of the Influenza Vaccines R&D Roadmap (IVR) Initiative and underscores the importance of improving vaccine performance and production. The review identifies key barriers to vaccine development and outlines priorities for advancing the influenza vaccine R&D enterprise. Without significant improvements, the next influenza pandemic may still be fought with outdated technology.

Of 110 participants enrolled, 103 were included in the per-protocol analysis (52 HD; 51 SD). title: UNIVERSAL EPIDEMIC SCALING: INFLUENZA AND COVID-19

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study addresses the challenge of parameterizing conventional compartmental models over multi-wave epidemic horizons, where susceptibility and transmission conditions change between successive epidemic regimes. The framework aims to provide a more adaptable approach to epidemic modeling.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study introduces a reduced macroscopic framework that shifts the scale of epidemic description from individual-level transmission structure to effective population-level dynamics. It evaluates the framework using comparative time-series data for SARS-CoV-2 and seasonal influenza A within the geographically and demographically consistent setting of Rhode Island.
analysis.methods: Epidemic waves are formulated as transport processes governed by deterministic boundaries, mass balance, and a small set of effective macroscopic parameters. The framework is designed to incorporate transmission resistance and external control measures at the macroscopic level.
analysis.main_results: The analyzed trajectories of SARS-CoV-2 and seasonal influenza A exhibit a common reduced asymptotic scaling form, despite their different biological and immunological regimes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The results support the use of a macroscopic, scale-reduced representation for cross-calibration of heterogeneous surveillance signals and analytical assessment of healthcare-system demand. The framework enables analytical estimation of epidemic trajectories and peak healthcare demand without computationally intensive numerical simulation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of more adaptable models for predicting epidemic trajectories and healthcare demand, which is crucial for public health preparedness and resource allocation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to comparative time-series data for SARS-CoV-2 and seasonal influenza A within a single geographic and demographic setting. The evidence is moderate as it relies on a single location and does not account for broader population variability.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a macroscopic framework for epidemic modeling that shifts the focus from individual-level transmission to effective population-level dynamics. It addresses the challenge of parameterizing conventional compartmental models over multi-wave epidemics, where susceptibility and transmission conditions change. The framework is evaluated using time-series data for SARS-CoV-2 and seasonal influenza A in Rhode Island, revealing a common asymptotic scaling form despite differing biological regimes. The results suggest that this approach can be used for cross-calibrating surveillance signals and estimating healthcare demand without intensive simulations. However, the study is limited to a single geographic and demographic setting, which may affect the generalizability of its findings. The framework's potential for improving public health preparedness and resource allocation is highlighted, though further validation across diverse pathogens and populations is needed.

analysis.scope_and_question: Therefore, it is necessary to report and review such a potentially fatal case.

analysis.summary_en: Therefore, it is necessary to report and review such a potentially fatal case. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected coinfection of C psittaci , influenza A H3N2 virus, and Klebsiella pneumoniae in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. However, the patient's imaging presentation was not coupled with viral pneumonia, which raised suspicion for other pathogens. Omadacycline and baloxavir marboxil were prescribed. The initial diagnosis focused on influenza A for his positive influenza A nucleic acid.

title: Near real-time data on the human neutralizing antibody landscape to influenza virus in summer of 2026 shows antigenic advance of H3N2 subclade K region D mutants and H1N1 D.3.1.1 Sa mutants

analysis.research_question_and_background: Abstract Human seasonal influenza evolves rapidly, necessitating twice yearly decisions about whether to update the strains in the vaccine.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population.
analysis.methods: To help inform this decision, we have been using high-throughput sequencing-based neutralization assays to make twice yearly measurements of how recent human sera neutralize current human H3N2 and H1N1 strains.
analysis.main_results: Here we provide the third installment in this series of measurements by reporting 47,851 titers representing neutralization of 148 viral strains by 325 human sera collected between April and August of 2026.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This paper is accompanied by an interactive summary ( https://jbloomlab.github.io/flu-seqneut-2026/summary.html ) that enables detailed exploration of the results, and all titer data are publicly available for further analysis to aid vaccine antigen selection and studies of viral evolution.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The supplied evidence does not clearly state a specific scientific or public-health implication.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Our measurements show that new H3N2 subclade K strains with mutations in antigenic region D and new H1N1 subclade D.3.1.1 strains with mutations in antigenic region Sa (such as G155E) have reduced neutralization by human sera, with notable heterogeneity in the impact of some of these mutations across sera from different individuals.

analysis.summary_en: Abstract Human seasonal influenza evolves rapidly, necessitating twice yearly decisions about whether to update the strains in the vaccine. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population. To help inform this decision, we have been using high-throughput sequencing-based neutralization assays to make twice yearly measurements of how recent human sera neutralize current human H3N2 and H1N1 strains. Here we provide the third installment in this series of measurements by reporting 47,851 titers representing neutralization of 148 viral strains by 325 human sera collected between April and August of 2026. This paper is accompanied by an interactive summary ( https://jbloomlab.github.io/flu-seqneut-2026/summary.html ) that enables detailed exploration of the results, and all titer data are publicly available for further analysis to aid vaccine antigen selection and studies of viral evolution. The supplied evidence does not clearly state a specific scientific or public-health implication. Our measurements show that new H3N2 subclade K strains with mutations in antigenic region D and new H1N1 subclade D.3.1.1 strains with mutations in antigenic region Sa (such as G155E) have reduced neutralization by human sera, with notable heterogeneity in the impact of some of these mutations across sera from different individuals.

title: Antigenic and Molecular Genetic Evolution of Influenza Viruses in Kazakhstan from 2017 to 2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the antigenic and molecular genetic evolution of influenza viruses in Kazakhstan from 2017 to 2025, as influenza viruses continuously evolve, necessitating sustained surveillance to monitor changes in virus circulation and vaccine relevance.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed influenza epidemiology and viral evolution in Kazakhstan across eight consecutive epidemic seasons (2017/18–2024/25) using data from the national influenza sentinel surveillance system, along with antigenic characterization, Sanger sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, and phylogenetic analysis.
analysis.methods: Influenza activity was almost undetectable during the 2020/21 season, followed by the re-emergence of A(H3N2)-dominated circulation in 2021/22. In 2022/23, influenza B predominated initially, followed by A(H1N1)pdm09, whereas A(H3N2) predominated in 2023/24.
analysis.main_results: A total of 199 A(H1N1)pdm09, 157 A(H3N2), 105 B/Victoria, and 16 B/Yamagata viruses were genetically characterized. A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses showed successive replacement of 6B-derived lineages, with descendants of 6B.1A.5a.2 predominating in the post-pandemic period. A(H3N2) viruses showed substantial genetic diversification, progressing from 3C.2a descendants to 3C.2a1b-related viruses and subsequently to 2a.3a.1/J.2 viruses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate substantial post-pandemic changes in influenza epidemic timing, subtype dominance, and genetic composition in Kazakhstan, while circulating viruses remained within globally recognized evolutionary lineages.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings highlight the importance of integrated epidemiological, genetic, and antigenic surveillance for detecting emerging variants, assessing vaccine relevance, and supporting timely influenza prevention and control measures.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on data from the national influenza sentinel surveillance system, which may have limitations in capturing the full genetic diversity of circulating viruses, and the evidence is moderate due to the reliance on observational data.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the antigenic and molecular genetic evolution of seasonal influenza viruses in Kazakhstan from 2017 to 2025. It highlights the dynamic changes in influenza subtype dominance and genetic composition over time, emphasizing the need for sustained surveillance to monitor vaccine relevance and guide prevention strategies. The research utilized data from the national influenza sentinel surveillance system, combined with antigenic characterization, Sanger sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, and phylogenetic analysis. Key results include the successive replacement of 6B-derived lineages in A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses and substantial genetic diversification in A(H3N2) viruses. The study found that B/Victoria viruses were replaced by V1A.3a.2 in later seasons. These findings demonstrate the importance of integrated surveillance for tracking influenza evolution and supporting public health interventions. However, the study's reliance on observational data limits the strength of its conclusions, and the evidence is considered moderate.
